It smelled of rust and regret. And tonight, it smelled of sugar. Specifically, a sickly, artificial sugar that permeated the air around the Derry Playhouse.

It was a museum I’d visited countless times, a place I’d drifted through, a silent observer of empires risen and fallen. I’d admired the stark beauty of the Egyptian sarcophagi, traced the intricate carvings on Mesopotamian tablets, and squinted at the faded frescoes of Pompeii, all from a respectful, but utterly detached, distance. I’d learned the dates, the materials, the theories – the facts, perfectly categorized and presented. But I hadn’t *felt* anything. Not really.

I’d been coming to the museum for nearly twenty years, ever since my grandfather, a historian obsessed with the tangible evidence of the past, had dragged me along, insisting I "understand the weight of history.” He’d been a man of dust and parchment, of brittle bones and eroded stone. He’d always said you could only truly grasp the past by holding it, by connecting with the remnants it left behind. I’d nodded politely, absorbed the facts, and kept my hands firmly in my pockets.

Today, though, something was different. A prickle of restlessness, a dull ache of dissatisfaction, had settled over me. The usual clinical efficiency of the museum felt oppressive, the rows of displayed artifacts sterile and lifeless. I was tired of the explanations, the dates, the layers of interpretation. I wanted… something more.

It was from the Uruk period, dating back to around 3200 BC – a time when writing was still in its infancy, a revolutionary invention transforming the way humans communicated. It was, in short, utterly unremarkable.

I traced the worn leather of the grimoire, its pages filled with the scrawled accounts of my ancestors, a lineage stretching back nearly fifteen hundred years.

My task, passed down through generations of my family, was to record not just events, but the *feel* of them. The texture of fear, the weight of grief, the fleeting warmth of joy – these were the things that truly mattered, the things that lingered long after the battles were fought and the kings were gone. Tonight, I was attempting to capture the essence of 1485, the year of Bosworth Field.

The rain, like this one, carried the stench of impending death. He wrote of the mud, thick and sucking at his boots, the endless grey sky, the distant rumble of armies.
